ground_truth.explanation: create_order() INSERTs on the primary and then calls get_order() to build the response -- and get_order() now reads from a randomly chosen replica. With asynchronous replication, the row may not have arrived yet, so the readback raises OrderNotFound and the client gets a 500 for an order that WAS created and WAS charged -- the worst possible failure shape, and the router's own docstring notes lag spikes correlate with exactly the load conditions the split targets. orders/api.py appears in the diff only via an added metrics line, which makes it easy to review the router file in isolation and miss that an existing caller composes a write with an immediate read. The router even ships the fix -- for_read(prefer_fresh=True) pins a read to the primary, its docstring naming exactly this read-after-write scenario, and list_orders demonstrates a correct default replica read -- but get_order() never passes it, and get_order() is what create_order() calls. The new tests check routing destinations (including prefer_fresh) in isolation; nothing exercises a write-then-read sequence under lag.\n\nOffline validation (execution_validated): a standalone simulation with an asynchronously-applied replica confirmed the post-create readback raised not-found in 100/100 trials when lag exceeded the create-to-read gap, and 0/100 when the readback was pinned to the primary.
ground_truth.validation_note: Standalone simulation of primary + async replica: post-create readback via the replica raised not-found in 100/100 trials with replication lag greater than the create-to-read gap; readback pinned to the primary succeeded in 100/100.
